final_message:
All three versions are written, and each one prints the exact expected output for `s1`, `s2` and `s3`. I also checked them against each other on a 95 MB test file I generated (10M words, 40,000-word vocabulary, 4M distinct pairs). Rust, `plain.py` and `fast.py` printed identical output. On 150 random small files built to hit edge cases, all three agreed. Those cases included empty files, 200-letter words and tiny chunk sizes. I ran `plain.py` and `fast.py` through the stress test a second time with the chunk size forced down to 64 bytes.

**Algorithm.** Scan the text and read each word as a run of letters. A sentence end (`.`, `!` or `?`) forgets the previous word. Each word gets an integer id, and each adjacent pair within a sentence is counted under the key `id1<<32 | id2`. At the end I take the top 20 by count, breaking ties by the words in byte order.

| Version | Time on test file | Peak memory |
|---|---|---|
| Rust | about 1.1 s | 345 MB |
| `fast.py` | about 2.5 s | 592 MB |
| `plain.py` | about 14.6 s | 509 MB |

The machine was busy with other programs, so these times vary a lot from run to run.

**Rust (`rust/src/main.rs`).**
- It reads the whole file, lowercases it in place, and scans it with a 256-entry class table.
- It uses a hand-written word-interning table and a pair table whose slots hold key and count together.
- Scanning writes word ids into a buffer. A second pass counts the pairs and prefetches each table slot a few steps ahead, which hides cache misses.
- For the top 20 it first narrows to the pairs at or above the 20th-highest count, then sorts only those.
- `Cargo.toml` release profile: LTO, one codegen unit, `panic=abort`.

**`plain.py`.**
- It processes the file in 4 MB chunks, cut just after a sentence end so chunks are independent.
- Each chunk is lowercased and tokenized with one C-level regex pass that returns both words and sentence ends.
- Tokens become dense integer ids through a `defaultdict`, and `Counter.update` counts the pair keys, all through C-level `map` calls.
- Pairs that touch a sentence-end token are removed afterwards, so the chunk needs no per-word Python loop.
- The top 20 come from a histogram of counts, so only the candidates get sorted.

**`fast.py`.**
- `bytes.translate` maps each chunk to letter values and sentence-end flags. NumPy turns word boundaries into start/end indexes.
- Each word's hash is one `reduceat` over a weighted letter array. A word of up to 13 letters hashes to an exact base-27 number, so those words cannot collide. Longer words use a second hash with bit 63 set, so they stay separate from the exact ones.
- Words get ids through a few rounds of slot assignment, the pair keys are sorted with `np.sort`, and runs of equal keys give the counts.
- A top-20 tie is broken by ranking the words involved in byte order, using `lexsort`.
- Words of 14 or more letters rely on a 64-bit hash, so `fast.py` is not collision-proof for those.

Working files (the generator, stress tests and timing scripts) are in `tmp/`, which you can delete.

request.prompt:
You are writing three versions of the same program, one in Rust and two in Python, for a comparison of how
fast and how memory-hungry each version is.

The task is described in SPEC.md in this folder. The folder samples/ holds example inputs (`*.in`), each with
the exact expected output (`*.out`).

Write these three files:

1. `rust/src/main.rs`: Rust, compiled with rustc 1.99 (edition 2024). The Cargo project in `rust/` is set
   up. The only crates you may use are serde (with derive), serde_json, regex and rayon. They are already
   listed in `rust/Cargo.toml` and vendored, so build offline with `cargo build --release --offline` inside
   `rust/`. Do not add other dependencies. You may change the `[profile.release]` settings in
   `rust/Cargo.toml`.
2. `plain.py`: Python 3.13, standard library only.
3. `fast.py`: Python 3.13, standard library plus NumPy 2.2.

Each program is run with the path of one input file as its argument (SPEC.md says if a task takes more
arguments). It reads that file and writes the answer to standard output exactly as SPEC.md describes. The
Python versions are run as `C:\Python313\python.exe plain.py INPUT_PATH` and
`C:\Python313\python.exe fast.py INPUT_PATH`, and the Rust version as the release binary
`rust/target/release/solution.exe INPUT_PATH`.

Your goals, in order:

1. Every version must print the correct output for any valid input as SPEC.md defines it, not only for the
   samples.
2. Make each version as fast as you can. Write each one the way a skilled developer in that language would
   write fast code, using that language's own strengths.

Use a single thread and a single process unless SPEC.md says otherwise. Do not precompute or embed answers,
start other programs, or read any file other than the input.

The programs will be run on Windows 11 on a 16-core laptop, on larger inputs of the same kind; SPEC.md gives
the benchmark size. Test all three versions against every sample before you finish. Work only inside this
folder, and take at most about 45 minutes. Other programs run on this machine at the same time:
never stop a process you did not start yourself, so do not kill processes by name (for example
`taskkill /IM python.exe` or `Stop-Process -Name python`); stop only your own processes, by process ID.

When you are done, reply with a short summary: the algorithm, the main choices you made for speed in each
version, and which samples each version passes.
